title: "Vision Transformers"
description: "An intro to vision transformers"
categories: [Modeling]
---

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="1. A minimal overview of transformers"}
At a high level, a transformer processes a sequence of vectors through repeated blocks that alternate between two operations:
1. information aggregation across tokens
2. feature transformation within each token

This simple pattern turns out to be extremely powerful.

---

*From tokens to embeddings*

The input first becomes a sequence of vectors.
For example, in vision: the image is split into patches, and each patch is projected into an embedding vector
$x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$
The model therefore operates on a matrix
$X = [x_1, x_2, ..., x_n] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$,
where: $n$ is number of tokens (patches) and $d$ is the embedding dimension

---

*Transformer blocks*

A transformer repeatedly applies blocks of the form: attention → MLP.
Conceptually, these perform two complementary operations.

*Attention: aggregating information across tokens*:
In the attention step, each token gathers information from other tokens.
$y_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j$,
where the weights are computed from token similarity:
$\alpha_{ij} =. \text{softmax}\left(\frac{q_i^T k_j}{\sqrt{d}}\right)$.
This means that each token becomes a **weighted combination of other tokens in the sequence**.
Importantly, the weights depend on the **content of the tokens themselves**,
so the aggregation pattern can change for every input.

*MLP: transforming features within each token*:
After attention mixes information across tokens,
a feed-forward network transforms each token independently:
$z_i = W_2 \sigma(W_1 y_i)$.
This step mixes information **within the feature dimension**, but does not combine tokens.

---

Stacking many such blocks allows information to propagate through the sequence
while repeatedly transforming the representation.
Despite this simplicity,
stacking these operations allows the model to represent complex relationships
between elements of the sequence.

---

*Residual structure*

In practice, each block is wrapped with residual connections and normalization:
$X' = X + \text{Attention}(\text{LN}(X))$,
$X'' = X' + \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(X'))$
This structure stabilizes training and allows many blocks to be stacked.


<!--
NOTES
While vision transformers were initially motivated by their ability to model long-range interactions,
their real advantage comes from flexible, content-dependent feature aggregation
and better scaling with data and model size.

CNN - ViT convergence

Modern CNNs (ConvNeXt, large kernel CNNs) have started moving toward more flexible aggregation:
	•	larger kernels
	•	dynamic convolutions
	•	attention-like modules

Meanwhile transformers are adding:
	•	locality bias
	•	hierarchical structure

Both paradigms are slowly converging
-->
